findings.description: The catalog_db RDS instance sets publicly_accessible = true, so the database receives a public endpoint reachable from the internet. Combined with the VPC-wide 3306 ingress rule and default username 'admin', this exposes the database to external attack and makes brute-force/credential-stuffing attempts reachable from anywhere.

storage_encrypted = false leaves the RDS database, its automated snapshots and underlying storage unencrypted. Any party with access to the storage layer or a snapshot copy can read the contents in cleartext.

The catalog app role policy grants s3:*, ec2:* and rds:* on Resource '*'. The role is attached to an EC2 instance, so a compromise of that instance yields full control over all buckets and databases in the account and the ability to manipulate EC2 resources (a privilege-escalation path).

The startup script writes the RDS password ('${var.password}') into /var/www/inc/dbinfo.inc in cleartext. Instance user_data is stored unencrypted in Terraform state and is readable from the instance metadata service, exposing the database credential to anyone with state access or the ability to query the instance.

The database security group permits MySQL (3306/tcp) from the entire VPC CIDR rather than from the specific application security group. Any instance in the VPC — including any compromised or untrusted workload — can reach the database directly, weakening network segmentation.

The database security group allows all protocols on all ports to 0.0.0.0/0. Unrestricted egress from a database tier enables data exfiltration and outbound command-and-control if the instance is compromised.
